items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: And Delaunay and Panassié worked very closely together interviewing American musicians

ctx.x: Yes certainly it was before LPs, but the idea of him spreading through recording.

Well that’s absolutely true, because people got to know the history of jazz that way, through LPs even more than those 78s that I just talked about, that started around 1940. And the fact that it was an organized series meant that people knew that they could expect another release the following month, and that way they were on the lookout. And the annotations that I wrote for the 78 RPM albums were the first group of written documentation of the careers of some of these performers, because before that there…

rather special reason that I didn’t catch on to at first, which was that the American jazz records that got released abroad tended to stay in the catalogues. They didn’t sell very widely and the record business was smaller in Europe than it was in America, and because they stayed in the catalogues they were there for reference as more and more people got interested in the historical recordings of the 1920s and early 30s.
